abstract: Individuals differ in their willingness to work for rewards. Although effort-based behavior shows trait-like stability and motivational traits associate with functional connectivity (FC), it remains unclear how robustly individual differences in effort are reflected in intrinsic FC of reward circuits. Here, we investigated whether effort-based behavior and questionnaire scores are reflected in nucleus accumbens (NAcc) FC. To this end, we evaluated this association in 84 healthy adults (43 women, 41 men), who completed five sessions of an effort allocation task and two task-free fMRI scans, each collected on different days to capture trait-like behavior and brain function. First, behavioral measures showed high test-retest reliability across sessions (ICCs: 0.62-0.83). Second, NAcc FC showed the highest reliability in subcortical regions (ICCs = 0.59-0.69), while cortical connections were heterogeneous and, overall, less reliable. Higher effort exertion was associated with stronger NAcc<>IFG FC (tmax(76) = 4.65, pFWE = .041, k = 141), while greater sensitivity to task difficulty was associated with stronger NAcc<>subcallosal gyrus FC (tmax(76) = -5.15, pFWE = .028, k = 155). Intriguingly, the association of effort exertion with NAcc<>IFG FC decreased over behavioral sessions, whereas the association of sensitivity to cost (difficulty) with NAcc<>subcallosal FC was stable over behavioral sessions. Our findings show that identifying robust brain-behavior associations likely requires comparable multi-session approaches, at least in moderately sized samples. Beyond reliability, such approaches may also help reveal additional insights about the temporal profile of brain-behavior associations, which may differ markedly for new versus routine task performance.
